statement: A research lab stores $4.8 \times 10^{15}$ bytes of data. Each hard drive it buys holds $6 \times 10^{12}$ bytes. How many drives are needed to hold all of the data?

choices.misconception: I divided the larger coefficient by the smaller one, $6 \div 4.8 = 1.25$, instead of $4.8 \div 6$, and then used $10^{3}$.
I got $0.8 \times 10^{3}$ but changed 0.8 to 8 without lowering the exponent, so I wrote $8 \times 10^{3}$.
I added the exponents 15 and 12 as if I were multiplying, then rewrote $0.8 \times 10^{27}$ as $8 \times 10^{26}$.

hints: Divide the total data by the size of one drive.
Divide the coefficients and the powers of ten separately. When dividing powers of ten, subtract the exponents.

solutions.reliable: Number of drives $= \dfrac{4.8 \times 10^{15}}{6 \times 10^{12}} = \dfrac{4.8}{6} \times 10^{15-12} = 0.8 \times 10^{3} = 800$. The quotient is a whole number, so exactly 800 drives hold the data. The idea: in scientific notation, divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents, then write the result in standard form.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
